(B) 25% is the ratio P<sub>max</sub>/(V²/R<sub>th</sub>), not the efficiency.
(D) 75% has no basis here; efficiency rises above 50% only when R<sub>L</sub> > R<sub>th</sub>.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q3 · Vol 5 p 1295
q: Three equal resistors of R ohms are connected in delta. The equivalent star resistance per phase is:
why: R<sub>Y</sub> = (R·R)/(R+R+R) = R/3.
wrong: (B) 3R is the reverse conversion (star → delta: R<sub>Δ</sub> = 3R<sub>Y</sub>).
(C) Resistance is not preserved in the conversion; only terminal behaviour is.
(D) √3 relates line and phase voltages in star, not resistance conversion.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q4 · Vol 5 p 1295
q: In a series RLC circuit at resonance, the power factor is:
why: At resonance X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub>, so the net impedance is purely R and current is in phase with voltage (pf = 1).
wrong: (A) 0.707 pf occurs at the half-power (band-edge) frequencies, where |X| = R.
(B) Zero leading pf occurs for a purely capacitive circuit.
(D) Zero lagging pf occurs for a purely inductive circuit.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q5 · Vol 5 p 1296
q: The quality factor (Q) of a series RLC circuit is:
why: Q = ω<sub>0</sub>L/R = (1/R)√(L/C) with ω<sub>0</sub> = 1/√(LC).
wrong: (A) √(LC) has units of time (1/ω<sub>0</sub>); dividing by R does not give a dimensionless Q.
(B) R√(L/C) increases with R, but Q of a series circuit falls as R increases.
(C) R√(C/L) is the Q of a parallel RLC circuit (inverse form).

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q6 · Vol 5 p 1296
q: The form factor of a pure sinusoidal wave is:
why: Form factor = RMS/Average = (V<sub>m</sub>/√2)/(2V<sub>m</sub>/π) = 1.11.
wrong: (A) 1.0 is the form factor of a square wave.
(B) 1.414 is the peak (crest) factor of a sine wave.
(D) 1.732 is the crest factor of a triangular wave.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q7 · Vol 5 p 1296
q: In the two-wattmeter method of 3-phase power measurement, one wattmeter reads zero. The power factor of the load is:
why: W<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub>cos(30°+φ) = 0 ⇒ φ = 60° ⇒ pf = cos60° = 0.5.
wrong: (A) At pf = 0.866 (φ = 30°) one meter reads half of the other, not zero.
(B) At pf = 0 the two readings are equal and opposite (total power zero), not one zero.
(D) At pf = 1 both wattmeters read equal positive values.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q8 · Vol 5 p 1296
q: A 230 V, 100 W lamp has a hot resistance of:
wrong: (B) 0.43 = P/V (the current in amperes), not resistance.
(C) 2.3 = 230/100, i.e. V/P, which is not a resistance formula.
(D) 52.9 Ω is a decimal-place error (dividing by 1000 instead of 100).

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q9 · Vol 5 p 1297
q: The capacitive reactance of a 10 µF capacitor at 50 Hz is approximately:
wrong: (A) 3.14 Ω results from multiplying by 2πfC instead of taking its reciprocal (×1000).
(C) 31.8 Ω is a factor-of-10 slip (using 100 µF).
(D) 3183 Ω corresponds to 1 µF, not 10 µF.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q10 · Vol 5 p 1297
q: In a balanced star-connected system with 400 V line voltage, the phase voltage is:
why: In star, V<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>/√3 = 400/1.732 ≈ 231 V.
wrong: (A) 133 V = 400/3; √3 is the correct divisor, not 3.
(B) V<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>L</sub> holds for delta connection, not star.
(D) 693 V = 400 × √3; multiplied instead of divided. Electrical Machines

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q11 · Vol 5 p 1297
q: A DC series motor should never be started without load because:
why: N ∝ E<sub>b</sub>/φ. At no load, armature (= field) current is tiny, so φ is very small and speed rises to dangerous values.
wrong: (A) Field current equals the (small) armature current at no load, so no overheating.
(C) At no load the current is actually very small, not high.
(D) Torque is small but not zero; the machine still accelerates.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q12 · Vol 5 p 1297
q: The EMF equation of a DC generator is (P = poles, Z = conductors, A = parallel paths, N in rpm):
why: Each conductor cuts Pφ flux per revolution; EMF per path = PφZN/(60A).
wrong: (A) Z (number of conductors) is missing, so it gives EMF of a single conductor per path at best.
(B) Omits A; it would hold only if A = 1, which no practical winding has (lap: A = P, wave: A = 2).
(D) P belongs in the numerator (more poles → more flux cut), not the denominator.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q13 · Vol 5 p 1298
q: The core of a transformer is laminated mainly to reduce:
why: Thin insulated laminations increase the resistance of eddy-current paths; eddy loss ∝ t² (lamination thickness).
wrong: (B) Leakage reactance depends on winding arrangement (interleaving), not lamination.
(C) Hysteresis loss is reduced by using silicon steel (low hysteresis coefficient), not by lamination.
(D) Copper loss depends on winding resistance and load current (I²R).

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q14 · Vol 5 p 1298
q: A transformer operates at maximum efficiency when:
why: Differentiating η with respect to load current gives the condition variable (Cu) loss = constant (core) loss.
wrong: (A) No such condition arises from dη/dI = 0.
(B) Iron loss is present whenever the transformer is energised; it can't be zero.
(C) Copper loss is zero only at no load, where output (and efficiency) is zero.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q15 · Vol 5 p 1298
q: The open-circuit (no-load) test on a transformer is used to determine:
why: With secondary open, current is small (copper loss negligible) and rated voltage is applied, so wattmeter reads core loss.
wrong: (A) Equivalent impedance comes from the SC test (Z<sub>eq</sub> = V<sub>sc</sub>/I<sub>sc</sub>).
(B) Equivalent series resistance comes from the SC test (R<sub>eq</sub> = P<sub>sc</sub>/I<sub>sc</sub>²).
(C) Full-load copper loss is found from the short-circuit test.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q16 · Vol 5 p 1298
q: The synchronous speed of a 4-pole, 50 Hz induction motor is:
wrong: (B) 3000 rpm is for a 2-pole machine.
(C) 1000 rpm is for a 6-pole machine.
(D) 750 rpm is for an 8-pole machine.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q17 · Vol 5 p 1299
q: A 4-pole, 50 Hz induction motor runs at 1440 rpm. The rotor current frequency is:
wrong: (B) 50 Hz is the rotor frequency only at standstill (s = 1).
(C) 48 Hz = f(1 − s), the stator-referred frequency equivalent of rotor speed, not rotor current frequency.
(D) 0.04 is the slip itself (dimensionless), not the frequency.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q18 · Vol 5 p 1299
q: The slip of a 3-phase induction motor at the instant of starting is:
why: At start rotor speed N = 0, so s = (N<sub>s</sub> − 0)/N<sub>s</sub> = 1.
wrong: (A) s = 0 means rotor at synchronous speed; no torque is produced.
(B) Negative slip means the rotor runs above N<sub>s</sub> (generator action).
(C) s = 0.5 means the rotor is at half synchronous speed.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q19 · Vol 5 p 1299
q: The maximum torque of an induction motor occurs when:
why: Torque T ∝ sR<sub>2</sub>/(R<sub>2</sub>² + s²X<sub>2</sub>²); dT/ds = 0 gives R<sub>2</sub> = sX<sub>2</sub>.
wrong: (A) R<sub>2</sub> = s is dimensionally inconsistent (ohms vs. ratio).
(B) R<sub>2</sub> = 0 gives zero torque.
(D) R<sub>2</sub> = X<sub>2</sub> is the condition for maximum torque at starting (s = 1) only.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q20 · Vol 5 p 1299
q: A 3-phase synchronous motor is not self-starting because:
o: (B) The average starting torque is zero
(D) The stator produces no rotating field
why: The rotor poles are alternately attracted and repelled by the fast-rotating stator field; due to inertia the average torque is zero.
wrong: (A) Slip is an induction-motor concept; slip = 1 in an induction motor actually gives starting torque.
(C) The DC field is excited; excitation doesn't make it self-starting.
(D) A balanced 3-phase stator does produce a rotating magnetic field.
ans: (B) The average starting torque is zero

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q21 · Vol 5 p 1300
q: An over-excited synchronous motor operates at:
why: Over-excitation makes E > V, so the motor supplies reactive power, i.e. draws leading current (synchronous condenser).
wrong: (A) Lagging pf occurs when under-excited.
(B) Unity pf occurs at normal excitation.
(D) Zero lagging pf corresponds to a pure inductor, not an over-excited motor.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q22 · Vol 5 p 1300
q: Voltage regulation of an alternator may be negative when supplying:
why: With leading current, armature reaction is magnetising, so terminal voltage rises above the no-load EMF ⇒ negative regulation.
wrong: (B) Lagging loads give demagnetising armature reaction ⇒ large positive regulation.
(C) Unity pf gives small positive regulation (resistive + reactive drop).
(D) At no load there is no load current, so regulation isn't defined/zero.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q23 · Vol 5 p 1300
q: Which of the following is NOT a necessary condition for parallel operation of alternators?
why: Alternators of different ratings can share load in proportion; equal kVA is not required.
wrong: (B) Unequal voltages cause heavy circulating currents — a necessary condition.
(C) Wrong phase sequence is a short circuit at synchronising — necessary.
(D) Unequal frequencies cause the machines to slip poles — necessary. Power Systems

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q24 · Vol 5 p 1300
q: The surge impedance of a lossless transmission line is:
why: Z<sub>c</sub> = √[(R + jωL)/(G + jωC)] → √(L/C) when R = G = 0.
wrong: (B) √(C/L) is the surge admittance (reciprocal).
(C) 1/√(LC) is the velocity of propagation.
(D) √(LC) is the time delay per unit length.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q25 · Vol 5 p 1301
q: Ferranti effect in a long transmission line refers to:
o: (B) Receiving-end voltage exceeding sending-end voltage at light load
(C) Current crowding at the conductor surface
why: At light load the charging current through the line inductance causes voltage rise at the receiving end.
wrong: (A) That is corona.
(C) That is skin effect.
(D) Voltage drop under heavy load is normal regulation, not Ferranti effect.
ans: (B) Receiving-end voltage exceeding sending-end voltage at light load

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q26 · Vol 5 p 1301
q: Corona loss on overhead lines can be reduced by:
o: (B) Increasing the conductor diameter (or using bundled conductors)
why: A larger effective radius reduces surface electric stress, raising the disruptive critical voltage.
wrong: (A) Smaller conductors increase surface stress and corona.
(C) Reduced spacing increases surface gradient and corona.
(D) Higher voltage beyond critical voltage increases corona loss (∝ (V − V<sub>d</sub>)²).
ans: (B) Increasing the conductor diameter (or using bundled conductors)

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q27 · Vol 5 p 1301
q: Skin effect is absent in a conductor carrying:
why: Skin effect is caused by changing flux linkages; with DC there is no change, so current distributes uniformly.
wrong: (A) Skin effect is most pronounced at high frequency.
(B) At 50 Hz skin effect exists (small but present).
(C) Stranding reduces but does not eliminate skin effect for AC.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q28 · Vol 5 p 1301
q: The most frequently occurring fault in a power system is:
why: About 70–80% of faults are single line-to-ground (e.g., insulator flashover, tree contact).
wrong: (A) LL faults are roughly 10–15%.
(C) 3-phase faults are the most severe but rarest (~5%).
(D) LLG faults are roughly 10%.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q29 · Vol 5 p 1302
q: Zero-sequence currents are absent in a:
why: Zero-sequence current requires a return path through ground/neutral; an LL fault doesn't involve ground.
wrong: (B) In an SLG fault I<sub>a0</sub> = I<sub>a1</sub> = I<sub>a2</sub>, so zero sequence is present.
(C) Any fault path to a grounded neutral permits zero-sequence current.
(D) LLG involves ground, so zero-sequence current flows.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q30 · Vol 5 p 1302
q: Base impedance in per-unit system is given by:
why: Z<sub>b</sub> = V<sub>b</sub>²/S<sub>b</sub>, and in kV and MVA the 10<sup>6</sup> factors cancel.
wrong: (B) This is base admittance.
(C) Voltage must be squared for dimensional consistency.
(D) Dimensionally incorrect.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q31 · Vol 5 p 1302
q: Buchholz relay is used to protect:
why: It is a gas-actuated relay placed in the pipe between the main tank and conservator; detects incipient internal faults.
wrong: (A) Alternators use differential, loss-of-excitation, negative-sequence relays etc.
(C) Lines use distance and over-current relays.
(D) Motors have no oil conservator; they use thermal/overload relays.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q32 · Vol 5 p 1302
q: The relay best suited for protection of long transmission lines is:
why: The Mho relay is inherently directional and least affected by power swings, ideal for long lines.
wrong: (B) Overcurrent relays lack selectivity on long lines where fault current varies little.
(C) Reactance relay suits short lines (unaffected by arc resistance).
(D) Impedance relay suits medium lines; it is non-directional.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q33 · Vol 5 p 1303
q: SF<sub>6</sub> gas is used in circuit breakers because it is:
why: SF<sub>6</sub> captures free electrons forming heavy negative ions, rapidly restoring dielectric strength.
wrong: (A) SF<sub>6</sub> is about 5 times heavier than air.
(B) SF<sub>6</sub> is non-inflammable and inert.
(C) A conductive medium would sustain, not quench, the arc.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q34 · Vol 5 p 1303
q: The equal area criterion is used to study:
o: (B) Steady-state stability of a multi-machine system
(C) Transient stability of a single machine connected to an infinite bus
why: It compares accelerating and decelerating areas under the P–δ curve to find the critical clearing angle.
wrong: (A) Voltage stability uses P–V / Q–V curves.
(B) It applies only to a single machine / two-machine system, and to transient, not steady-state stability.
(D) Frequency control is Load Frequency Control, unrelated.
ans: (C) Transient stability of a single machine connected to an infinite bus

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q35 · Vol 5 p 1303
q: In a load flow study, the quantities specified at the slack (swing) bus are:
why: The slack bus supplies the system losses, so voltage magnitude and angle (reference, δ = 0) are fixed.
wrong: (A) P and |V| are specified at generator (PV) buses.
(B) P and Q are specified at load (PQ) buses.
(D) No bus type specifies Q and δ. Control Systems

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q36 · Vol 5 p 1303
q: For G(s)H(s) = K / [s²(s + 2)], the type and order of the system are:
why: Type = number of poles at origin = 2; order = highest power of s in denominator = 3.
wrong: (A) There are two poles at the origin (s²), not one.
(C) Type and order are interchanged.
(D) The pole at s = −2 also counts toward order, making it 3.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q37 · Vol 5 p 1304
q: The steady-state error of a Type-1 system for a unit step input is:
why: For Type 1, K<sub>p</sub> = ∞, so e<sub>ss</sub> = 1/(1 + K<sub>p</sub>) = 0.
wrong: (B) 1/K<sub>v</sub> is the error for a ramp input.
(C) Infinite step error does not occur for any stable closed-loop type ≥ 0.
(D) This is the general formula; it's finite only for Type 0.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q38 · Vol 5 p 1304
q: A second-order system is critically damped when the damping ratio ζ is:
why: At ζ = 1 the roots are real and equal – fastest response without overshoot.
wrong: (A) 0 < ζ < 1 is underdamped (overshoot).
(C) ζ > 1 is overdamped (sluggish, real distinct roots).
(D) ζ = 0 is undamped (sustained oscillation).

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q39 · Vol 5 p 1304
q: In the Routh–Hurwitz criterion, the number of sign changes in the first column indicates:
o: (A) Number of roots on the jω-axis
(B) Number of roots in the left half of the s-plane
(D) Number of roots in the right half of the s-plane
why: Each sign change corresponds to one closed-loop pole with a positive real part.
wrong: (A) jω-axis roots are indicated by a row of zeros, not sign changes.
(B) Left-half roots correspond to no sign changes.
(C) Order equals the number of rows minus one.
ans: (D) Number of roots in the right half of the s-plane

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q40 · Vol 5 p 1304
q: Gain margin is evaluated at the:
why: At phase crossover the phase is −180°; GM = 1/|G(jω<sub>pc</sub>)H(jω<sub>pc</sub>)|.
wrong: (A) At gain crossover (|GH| = 1) the phase margin is measured.
(B) Resonant frequency is where closed-loop magnitude peaks (M<sub>r</sub>).
(C) Corner frequency is a Bode asymptote break point.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q41 · Vol 5 p 1305
q: A lag compensator is mainly used to:
o: (A) Increase phase margin by adding phase lead
why: It raises low-frequency gain (acts as low-pass), reducing steady-state error.
wrong: (A) Adding phase lead is the job of a lead compensator.
(B) It slows the transient response.
(D) Lag compensation reduces bandwidth. Electronics & Power Electronics

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q42 · Vol 5 p 1305
q: For a thyristor (SCR), the latching current is:
why: Latching current (to stay ON right after triggering) is typically 2–3 times the holding current.
wrong: (B) Holding current is the smaller one – minimum to remain ON once conducting.
(C) A finite anode current is needed to latch.
(D) They are different parameters with different values.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q43 · Vol 5 p 1305
q: The ripple factor of a single-phase full-wave rectifier (resistive load) is:
wrong: (A) Zero ripple would be pure DC; not possible without filtering.
(B) 1.11 is the form factor, not the ripple factor.
(D) 1.21 is the ripple factor of a half-wave rectifier.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q44 · Vol 5 p 1305
q: A chopper is a:
why: It converts fixed DC to variable DC by switching (duty-cycle control).
wrong: (A) DC to AC is an inverter.
(C) AC to AC (frequency change) is a cycloconverter; AC voltage controller keeps frequency.
(D) AC to DC is a rectifier.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q45 · Vol 5 p 1306
q: The function of a freewheeling diode in a controlled rectifier with RL load is to:
o: (B) Prevent negative output voltage and improve input power factor
why: It provides a path for inductive current when the voltage reverses, so output doesn't go negative; this also improves pf.
wrong: (A) Firing angle is set by the gate circuit, not by the diode.
(C) It keeps load current flowing (continuous), not zero.
(D) It actually reduces ripple and makes load current smoother.
ans: (B) Prevent negative output voltage and improve input power factor

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q46 · Vol 5 p 1306
q: An ideal op-amp has input impedance of:
why: Ideal op-amp draws no input current, so Z<sub>in</sub> = ∞.
wrong: (A) Ideal output impedance is zero, so they cannot be equal.
(B) Zero is the ideal output impedance.
(D) A finite value like 1 kΩ is non-ideal.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q47 · Vol 5 p 1306
q: A Zener diode is mainly used as a:
why: In reverse breakdown, the voltage across a Zener stays nearly constant over a wide current range.
wrong: (A) A two-terminal diode cannot amplify; transistors do.
(B) Oscillators need gain and feedback.
(D) Ordinary PN diodes are used for rectification.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q48 · Vol 5 p 1306
q: The phase shift between input and output in a common-emitter amplifier is:
why: An increase in base current increases collector current, increasing drop across R<sub>C</sub> and lowering V<sub>CE</sub> ⇒ inversion.
wrong: (A) 90° doesn't occur in a resistive-loaded single stage amplifier at mid-band.
(C) 0° phase shift is for common-base and common-collector configurations.
(D) 360° is equivalent to 0° and doesn't describe CE. Measurements & Instrumentation

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q49 · Vol 5 p 1307
q: A Megger is used to measure:
why: A Megger applies high DC voltage (500 V–5 kV) and reads resistances in megaohms.
wrong: (A) Currents are measured by clamp meters/ammeters.
(C) Inductance is measured by Maxwell/Hay/Anderson bridges.
(D) Low resistance is measured by Kelvin double bridge.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q50 · Vol 5 p 1307
q: Kelvin's double bridge is used to measure:
why: The double-arm arrangement eliminates the effect of lead and contact resistances.
wrong: (A) High resistance uses Megger or loss-of-charge method.
(B) Capacitance uses Schering/De Sauty bridge.
(C) Medium resistance uses Wheatstone bridge.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q51 · Vol 5 p 1307
q: A PMMC instrument can measure:
why: Torque ∝ instantaneous current; on AC the average torque is zero, so it reads only DC (without a rectifier).
wrong: (A) RF measurement uses thermocouple instruments.
(B) Moving-iron instruments measure both AC and DC.
(C) With AC the pointer just vibrates about zero.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q52 · Vol 5 p 1307
q: Creeping in an induction-type energy meter is prevented by:
o: (D) Drilling two diametrically opposite holes in the disc
why: When a hole comes under the shunt magnet pole, eddy-current distortion creates a torque that stops the disc at no load.
wrong: (A) Shading band is used for lag/pf adjustment.
(B) The brake magnet provides braking torque proportional to speed, not anti-creep.
(C) Over-voltage actually causes creeping.
ans: (D) Drilling two diametrically opposite holes in the disc

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q53 · Vol 5 p 1308
q: Schering bridge is used to measure:
why: It measures unknown capacitance and its dissipation factor (tan δ), especially for insulation testing.
wrong: (B) High-Q inductance → Hay's bridge.
(C) Mutual inductance → Campbell/Heaviside bridge.
(D) Frequency → Wien bridge. Utilization & Miscellaneous

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q54 · Vol 5 p 1308
q: The SI unit of luminous intensity is:
why: Candela is the base SI unit of luminous intensity (lumen per steradian).
wrong: (A) Lumen is luminous flux.
(C) Lux is illuminance (lumen/m²).
(D) Lumen/W is luminous efficacy of a lamp.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q55 · Vol 5 p 1308
q: The motor most suitable for electric traction is the:
o: (D) Squirrel-cage induction motor with DOL starter
why: It gives very high starting torque and naturally slows under heavy load (constant-power characteristic).
wrong: (A) Synchronous motor is not self-starting and runs at constant speed.
(C) Shunt motor has near-constant speed and moderate starting torque.
(D) DOL cage motors have poor starting torque per ampere and no simple speed control.

src: Question bank · Practice MCQs · Q56 · Vol 5 p 1308
q: Heating of non-conducting materials such as wood or plastic is done by:
why: A high-frequency electric field causes dielectric loss inside the insulating material, heating it uniformly.
wrong: (A) Arc heating is for melting metals (arc furnaces).
(C) Direct resistance heating needs current through the material.
(D) Induction heating needs a conducting (usually magnetic) charge for eddy currents.
